---
title: "Coordinate coarsening"
description: "When eco generalises the coordinates of a table, how, and what a user should do about it."
---

```{r}
#| label: counts
#| include: false
m <- read.csv("../metadata/metadata.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
n_all <- nrow(m)
n_coarse <- sum(as.logical(m$coordinates_coarsened), na.rm = TRUE)
n_exact <- sum(grepl("_exact_", m$table))
```

Many eco tables give the location of every site, camera or trap. For a
threatened species, a list of exact locations can help a poacher, a collector or
a careless visitor. So for some tables eco publishes coordinates that are
coarser than the source's. This page sets out when that happens and what it
means for you. The binding text is clause E7 of the [standard](standard.html);
this page is a summary of it.

At present `r n_coarse` of `r n_all` tables have coarsened coordinates. Each
one is marked on [Browse the tables](data.html).

## The rule in one paragraph

eco never publishes coordinates more precise than the source did. When a table
includes a *flagged* taxon, or sites on private or community land, and the
source's coordinates are finer than 0.1 degree, eco snaps them to the centre of
their 0.1-degree grid cell (about 11 km north to south). The uncertainty column
is set to the half-diagonal of that cell, and the table's metadata records that
the coordinates were coarsened and how. Coordinates are coarsened, never
dropped: spatial occupancy and capture-recapture models need them, and a 10 km
cell is also what GBIF publishes for sensitive taxa.

## When a taxon is flagged

A taxon is flagged when any of these holds:

1. **The source says so.** The deposit, in its own text about the data, says the
   locations are sensitive or withheld, or that the taxon is protected or
   threatened. A word in a paper's title is not enough.
2. **IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable**, and the
   survey is within the taxon's native range. An introduced population, such as
   a garden escape or an invasive, is not flagged by its global category, so its
   coordinates are kept as the source published them.
3. **A national red list that the source cites lists it.**

The rule applies whoever published the source, government agencies included.
The exact coordinates remain one link away at the source. eco's job is not to
make them easier to find, filter and combine across hundreds of tables, and 0.1
degree costs little for most models.

## Private and community land

Coordinates finer than 0.1 degree are also coarsened, whatever the taxa, when
the source says the sites are on private land or community land, or on land
reached under an agreement with landowners or a community. The exception is
when the source says the landowners agreed to the locations being published.
The trigger is always the source's own statement about the data: eco never
infers land tenure from a map, a place name or the kind of study. If the
source says which sites are on such land, only those are coarsened. Otherwise
the whole table is.

## How different kinds of table are handled

- **Tables with only some flagged taxa.** Two tables ship. The full table, with
  coarsened coordinates, keeps the table's name. A second table drops the
  flagged taxa and keeps the source's precision; its name has `_exact` before
  the type suffix (for example `stallings_2025_gulfreefs_exact_count`). You
  choose which to use. Nothing the source published is lost. There are
  currently `r n_exact` `_exact` tables. Private-land coarsening has no `_exact`
  table, because the reason is the place rather than a taxon.
- **Projected coordinates** (metres on a national grid) are snapped to the
  centre of a 10 km cell of the source's grid, with an uncertainty of 7,071 m.
- **Trap arrays for spatial capture-recapture.** Coarsening individual traps
  would destroy the distances between them, which are what the model uses. For
  a flagged taxon, eco instead recentres the trap coordinates on the array, in
  local metres with the mean trap position at zero. The array's own location is
  given as a 0.1-degree cell, and `crs` is `local`.
- **Other location clues.** In a coarsened table, elevations are rounded to the
  nearest 100 m. Columns that name a place, such as a locality or site name, are
  not shipped, and a unit identifier that names a place is replaced by the
  source's code or a sequential id. The `_exact` table keeps them as published.
- **Coordinates the source already displaced** for privacy are shipped as
  published, and the metadata says how the source displaced them.

## Where to see it in a table

- The `coordinatesCoarsened` field of the table's metadata has `value` (true or
  false) and `method`, a sentence saying what was done and why. If a listed
  taxon was not coarsened (an introduced population, say), `method` says why.
  `rule` says which trigger applied: `taxon`, `private_land`, or both.
- `unit_coordinateUncertaintyInMeters` gives the uncertainty for each unit.
- The table's tags and its entry on [Browse the tables](data.html) say that its
  coordinates are coarsened. Some tables also have a [data note](data_notes.html).

## What we ask of users

**Do not try to recover coarsened coordinates.** Do not reconstruct them from
the source, from other datasets or from other eco tables, and do not join eco
tables to anything that would. If your research really needs the exact
locations, contact the people who collected the data, as described in
[Using eco responsibly](use.html).

**If you collected the data** and want the locations handled differently, open an
[issue](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/issues).
